coredata.dc:description: A Pseudomonas chlororaphis was found to degrade and utilize apolyester polyurethane as a sole carbon and energy source. Polyurethane utilization by P.chlororaphis followed simple Michaelis–Menten kinetics. The K s and μ max values were 0.802 mg·ml−1 and 1.316 doublings·h−1, respectively. The enzymes from P. chlororaphis responsible for polyurethanedegradation were found to be extracellular. Analysis of the polyurethane degrading proteins, usingnon-denaturing polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, revealed three active protein bands with R f values of 0.25, 0.417 and 0.917. A polyurethane degrading enzyme was purifiedand displayed esterase activity. This enzyme was inhibited by phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride andhad a molecular weight of 27,000 daltons.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: A Pseudomonas chlororaphis was found to degrade and utilize apolyester polyurethane as a sole carbon and energy source. Polyurethane utilization by P.chlororaphis followed simple Michaelis–Menten kinetics. The K s and μ max values were 0.802 mg·ml−1 and 1.316 doublings·h−1, respectively. ce:section.ce:para: The term polyurethanes refers to a class of polymers that has found widespread commercialapplications. Polyurethanes are an important and versatile class of man-made polymers used in a widevariety of products including paints and coatings, padding and thermal insulating materials. Thispolymer represents the first industrially important and commercially useful culmination of an old lineof organic research (namely, isocyanates). A polyurethane is a polymer in which the repeating unitis a urethane linkage. The urethane linkage results most readily through the reaction of the isocyanatefunction with an alcohol group. Urethanes are esters or amide esters of carbonic acid. However, thechemical term urethane is devoid of meaning and is better described as ethyl carbamate (H2NCO2C2H5).

Despite its xenobiotic origins, polyurethane has been found to be susceptible to biodegradationby naturally occurring microorganisms (Pathiranar and Seal, 1984; Bentham et al., 1987; Kay et al., 1991). Enzymatic attack on polyurethanes could be contributed byhydrolases such as ureases, proteases and esterases (Evans and Levisohn, 1968; Hole, 1972; Flip, 1978; Griffin, 1980). Indeed, proteolytic enzymes (papain and urease)and cholesterol esterase have been shown to degrade polyurethanes in vitro (Phua et al., 1987; Santerre et al., 1994).

Several reports have appeared in the literature on the susceptibility of polyurethanes to fungalattack. Mechanisms for this susceptibility have been suggested by Darby and Kaplan (1968)and Kaplan et al. (1968), who have shown that polyester-type polyurethanes are moresusceptible to fungal attack than other forms. Four species of fungi, Curvularia sengalensis,Fusarium solani, Aureobasidium pullulans and Cladosporium sp. wereisolated by Crabbe et al., 1994with the capability of degrading an ester-based polyurethane (ImpranilTM DLN). C. sengalensis was found to secrete an extracellular enzymewith esterase properties. This enzyme had a molecular weight of 28 kDa and was inhibited byphenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF).

This report describes the growth of a polyurethane-degrading bacterium, Pseudomonaschlororaphis, at the expense of the same heterogeneous polyurethane, ImpranilTMDLN and the purification and characterization of an Impranil degrading enzyme from P.chlororaphis.

P. chlororaphis was isolated, identified and obtained from the Naval ResearchLaboratory, Washington, D.C. by its ability to degrade a water dispersible polyurethane. P.chlororaphis was grown at 30°C with constant shaking on the yeast extract salts (YES)medium previously describe by Crabbe et al., 1994. Three stock solutions were prepared forYES media: Solution A (50×), 50 g K2HPO4 and 25 g KH2PO4 per liter; Solution B (100×) 50 g MgSO4·7H2O per liter andSolution C (1000×) 1.0 g MnCl2·4H2O, 14 mg CuCl2·2H2O, 11 mg ZnCl2, 20 mg CoCl2·6H2O, 13 mg Na2Mo4·2H2O and 75 mg FeCl3·6H2O per 500 ml.Solutions B and C were filter sterilized and stored at room temperature. Solution A was diluted 1:50with distilled water and supplemented with 0.4 g NH4Cl, 4.0 g gelatin (DIFCO) and 20 mg yeast extract per liter. After the resulting solution was autoclaved and cooled, solution B (10 ml/l), solution C (1.0 ml/l) and Impranil DLN (3 g/l) were added to complete the YES medium;the final pH was 7.2.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Determination of number of bacterial cells
ce:section.ce:para: P. chlororaphis cell number was determined using a Coulter Multisizer IIeinstrument (Coulter Scientific Instruments, Inc., Hialeah, FL) fitted with a 30 mm aperture. TheCoulter Multisizer IIe determines the number and size of particles suspended in a conductive liquidon either side of a small aperture, through which a suspension of the particles is forced to flow. Aseach particle passes through the aperture, it changes the impedance between the electrodes andproduces an electrical pulse of short duration having a magnitude essentially proportional to theparticle volume. The series of pulses is electronically scaled, counted and accumulated in a numberof sized-related channels which, when their contents are displayed on the integral visual display,produces a size distribution curve.

A 1 l culture of P. chlororaphis was incubated for 5 days in Impranil supplementedYES media. At the end of 5 days of incubation, little visible Impranil remained and the culture solidswere removed by centrifugation at 10,000×g for 20 min at 4°C. All remaining manipulationswere conducted at 4°C. The culture supernatant was brought to 60% saturation by the addition ofsolid ammonium sulfate. After 30 min of stirring, the precipitated proteins were collected bycentrifugation at 10,000×g for 15 min, resuspended in 50 mM phosphate buffer, pH 6.8,and dialyzed against 4 l of the same buffer overnight.

The crude enzyme preparation was applied to a DEAE Sepharose CL-6B column (3×14 cm)equilibrated with 50 mM phosphate buffer at pH 6.8 and developed in the same buffer at a flow rateof 1.0 ml·min−1. Two peaks of protein activity were detected in the void volume.Fractions associated with polyurethanase activity were collected and concentrated by ultrafiltrationwith a centriprep-10 concentrator (Amicon). The second peak depicting enzyme activity was furtherfractionated by gel filtration on Sephadex G75-120 (1.5×33 cm) equilibrated with 50 mMphosphate buffer, pH 6.8 The polyurethanase was estimated to be purified to 95% homogeneity byND–PAGE.

After each stage of the purification process, the purity of the enzyme was assessed bypolyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE). Non-denaturing (ND) gels were run with a 12%polyacrylamide resolving gel as described by Calza et al. (1985). Sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS)–PAGE was performed as described by Laemmli (1970)with a 12% polyacrylamideresolving gel. Proteins were visualized by Coomassie blue staining.

During the purification, aliquots of the protein fractions were spotted on YES agar platessupplemented with Impranil at pH 6.8 and examined for zones of clearing at 30°C. Assays todetermine the proteolytic activity of the enzyme used hide powder azure in 50 mM phosphate bufferat pH 6.8 (Chavira et al., 1984). Activity against hide powder azure was determined bymonitoring the increase in absorbance at 595 nm. One unit of activity was defined as the amount ofenzyme that changes the absorbance at 595 nm by 0.01·min−1. In addition, the enzymewas assayed for esterase activity by its ability to release r-nitrophenol from 8 mMr-nitrophenolacetate in 50 mM phosphate buffer, pH 6.8 at 30°C (Deshpande et al., 1984).One unit of esterase activity was defined as the amount of enzyme that produced 1 mmole ofr-nitrophenol per minute. All enzyme assays were observed to be linear with respect to time andprotein concentration under the tested conditions.

Impranil zymograms were carried out by using an ND–PAGE gel overlaid on a 0.7% (w/v)agarose gel containing 0.1% (v/v) Impranil in 50 mM phosphate buffer, pH 6.8. The zymogram wasincubated for 12 to 18 hr at 30°C. The polyacrylamide gel was removed and the agarose gelexamined for clear activity bands.
Protein concentration was determined by measuring A230/A260 accordingto Kalb and Bernlohr (1977).

P. chlororaphisThe ability of P. chlororaphis to degrade the water dispersiblepolyurethane, Impranil, was tested by measuring the zone of clearing around colonies grown in YESmedium. After an appropriate incubation period at 30°C, the agarose media was examined for zonesof clearing around colonies. Hydrolysis of the substrate could be visualized after approximately 16 h of incubation. This complete clearing was termed beta clearing. A second discrete zone of clearing,termed alpha, was observed distal to the beta clearing. This zone was only weakly translucent andrepresented a region of partial clearing of the polyurethane.

Optimal conditions for Impranil hydrolysis by P. chlororaphis were elucidated atdifferent temperatures and pH. P. chlororaphis was capable of hydrolyzing the Impranilsubstrate at ambient temperature and 30°C with little difference in the size of the zone of clearing ateither temperature (data not shown). No apparent growth occurred above 35°C. In addition, P.chlororaphis hydrolyzed the Impranil substrate at pH 5, 6, 7 and 8 with preeminent activity atpH 7 and 8, zones of clearing 38 mm and 42 mm, respectively. No activity was noted at pH 9 (data not shown). In addition, cell-free culture supernatant was also applied to Impranil agaroseplates. Zones of clearing were observed from cultural supernatant. Zones of clearing produced bycell-free extracts were markedly inhibited in the presence of 1 mM PMSF, but were unaffected byheating the extracts at 100°C for 10 min (data not shown).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Growth of P. chlororaphis on Impranil
ce:section.ce:para: Since Impranil is a colloidal suspension and strict limitations are placed on the knowledge ofits chemistry, conventional methods are impeded in determining the changes occurring during itsdegradation and growth of the bacterial cells utilizing it as a substrate. Thus, the Coulter instrument,Multisizer IIe, was employed to measure the change in bacterial number as the microorganism utilizedthe Impranil substrate. Increase in bacterial cell numbers were accomplished in the first 9 h ofincubation with a concentration reaching 2.4×109 cells·ml−1. Values forK s and μ max for polyurethane utilization by P.chlororaphis were elucidated by varying the Impranil concentration in the YES medium from0.5 mg·ml−1 to 3.0 mg·ml−1. Polyurethane utilization by P.chlororaphis followed simple Michaelis–Menten kinetics [Fig. 1 (A)]. From these results, the values of K s and μ max forpolyurethane were estimated from the least-squares regression analysis of Lineweaver–Burke plots [Fig. 1 (B)]. The values for K s and μ max were 0.802 mg·ml−1 and 1.316 doublings·h−1, respectively. The generation time for thegrowth of P. chlororaphis utilizing Impranil was calculated to be 45 min by taking theinverse of μ max.

Table 1 reveals that the second purified polyurethanase conferred only esterase activity and no proteaseactivity was exhibited. This is in contrast to the first peak of polyurethanase activity that wasobserved. However, both activities were inhibited with 1 mM PMSF. The purified esterase activitywas reduced by 55% by PMSF. The purified esterase was optimally active at pH 7.5 and was notinhibited by heating to 100°C for 10 min. The pH optimum determined on the polyurethane agaroseplates with crude enzyme was between 7 and 8.

Polyurethanes have found widespread acceptance for a variety of applications. Because ofshortages in raw materials for the synthesis of plastics, recycling of waste plastics has become veryimportant. Due to the incompatibility of most polymers and the enormous difficulties encountered insegregating polymeric articles of different chemical composition found in plastic waste, completerecycling is difficult and limited to special cases. Therefore, hydrolytic processes are being developedfor the utilization of plastics scrap and waste as either an energy source or as raw material for theproduction of valuable chemicals (Schnabel, 1981).

Different patterns of degradation observed by fungi with different samples of polyurethaneswere attributed to the many properties of polyurethanes such as topology and chemical composition (Pathiranar and Seal, 1983). In addition, synthetic polymers generally have short repeatingunits. The regularity in synthetic polymers allows the polymer chains to pack easily, resulting in theformation of crystalline regions. This limits the accessibility of the polymer chains to enzymes. Huang and Roby (1986)observed polyurethane degradation proceeding in a selective manner, withthe amorphous regions being degraded prior to the crystalline regions. It was also observed thatpolyurethanes with long repeating units and hydrophilic groups would be less likely to pack into highcrystalline regions as normal polyurethanes and these polymers were more accessible tobiodegradation.

Studies investigating degradation of polyurethane are often examined over a period of weeksto months (Pathiranar and Seal, 1985; Wales and Sagar, 1988; Dale and Squirrel, 1990). By using agar plates containing a colloidal, polyester–polyurethane, Impranil DLN,the degradation can be studied over a period of hours. In the present study, stationary growth of P. chlororaphis utilizing Impranil as the sole carbon and energy source was observed within ninehours in batch culture. The generation time for this bacterium was calculated to be 45 min. When thebacterium was grown on Impranil agar plates, zones of clearing were observed within eighteen hours.Two types of clearing zones were observed by P. chlororaphis grown on Impranil plates:beta, or complete clearing and alpha, or incomplete clearing. These zones of clearing were alsoobserved for the fungal isolate, C. senegalensis (Crabbe et al., 1994).

Cell-free supernatants of P. chlororaphis contained three distinct polyurethanaseactivities, as revealed by ND–PAGE zymograms. These three enzyme activities conferred beta zonesof clearing. However, the polyurethanase protein that was purified conferred an alpha zone of clearingand esterase activity, while protease activity was associated with beta clearing. The purified esterasehad a molecular mass of 27,000 Da and was inhibited by the serine protease inhibitor, PMSF. Theseresults are similar to those of the esterase purified from C. senegalensis (Crabbe et al., 1994).

Hole, 1972hypothesized that enzymatic attack on polyurethanes could includeproteases attacking the amide and urethane bonds, esterases hydrolyzing the many ester bonds andureases attacking the urea units. Indeed, proteolytic enzymes (papain and urease) and cholesterolesterase have been shown to degrade polyurethanes in vitro (Phua et al., 1987; Santerre et al., 1994). Interestingly, g-chymotrypsin could also hydrolyze Impranil on anagarose plate but neither a-chymotrypsin nor trypsin was capable of hydrolyzing the Impranilsubstrate (data not shown). In a previous study from this lab, a polyurethanase conferring proteolyticactivity was purified from Pseudomonas fluorescens (Howard and Blake, 1997,manuscript submitted for publication). The native molecular mass of this protein, as estimated byZimm plot analysis, was 116,000, while under denaturing conditions, SDS–PAGE, the molecularweight was 29,000. This suggests that this protein resides as a tetramer. Similarly, the proteolyticprotein conferred beta clearing and was inhibited by PMSF.

The enzymology as well as the biochemistry of the remaining polyurethanase proteinsproduced by P. chlororaphis are currently under investigation. These proteins will beassayed for both esterase and protease specificity as well as endopolyurethanase andexopolyurethanase activities in correlation with the beta and alpha clearing. In addition, genomiclibraries are being constructed to isolate the genes responsible for each polypeptide involved inpolyurethane degradation.
